children: shares fell more than 1.5% Tuesday as two additional news organizations deepened the legal fight over AI training data. The Seattle Times and Newsday are suing Microsoft and OpenAI, alleging their paywalled journalism was used to train AI models.
The claims add to litigation involving The New York Times (NYT) and Ziff Davis, turning isolated copyright disputes into a broader risk for Microsoft's AI strategy.
Why the Lawsuits Matter for Microsoft Stock

The unusual wrinkle is that The Seattle Times and Newsday previously joined an AI partnership initiative. Both received funding from the $10 million AI Collaborative and Fellowship Grant to hire AI fellows. That relationship makes questions about permission, licensing, and the boundaries of collaboration important.

For investors, the financial impact remains uncertain. Microsoft is large enough to absorb legal expenses, and its cloud and software businesses are not dependent on one publisher group. The risk is precedent.

If courts determine that paywalled articles require compensation or explicit licensing before being used for model training, AI development could become more expensive. Settlements could also encourage additional publishers to pursue claims, while restrictions on training data could complicate how OpenAI improves future models.

The stock's modest gain of 0.26% over the past year suggests investors are already demanding clearer returns from Microsoft's enormous AI spending. Fresh legal uncertainty adds another issue to that debate, even if Tuesday's decline cannot be attributed entirely to the lawsuits.

Microsoft also faces a separate consumer concern around Grand Theft Auto VI. Questions remain about how the highly anticipated game will perform on the less powerful Xbox Series S, with reports warning of possible performance drawbacks in intense situations.

That gaming issue is smaller than the AI dispute, but both highlight the same investor concern: Microsoft must convert major technology bets into growth while controlling legal, technical, and reputational risks.

title: Microsoft's OpenAI Partnership Draws Fresh Legal Fire
